text: Bush fires reported burning north of Sudbury, Ont., August 3, 1907. Settlers are fleeing to the lake shore with what they can carry, and there is no word yet from the outlying lumber camps.
label: wildfire

text: CHAPLEAU, Ont., June 24, 1908. — A despatch received late Tuesday states that the forest fire which had been smouldering in the timber limits west of the town for a fortnight was driven by a strong south-west wind on Monday afternoon and swept across the railway line in two places. The section men at Mile 34 escaped on a hand car with their families. Three bunkhouses and a large quantity of cut pulpwood were consumed. Smoke hangs so thick over the district that lamps were lit at noon. The rangers report that rain is badly needed, the woods being as dry as tinder after six weeks without a shower.
label: wildfire

text: Fire rangers in the Algoma district have been fighting a serious bush fire since the 12th of July, 1912. Several homesteads near Thessalon have been burned out and the settlers are camped in the open with their stock. Provisions are being sent up from the Soo by boat, and the rangers have asked the railway to stop all slash burning along the line until the weather breaks.
label: wildfire

text: Prairie fire. On the night of October 9, 1905, a grass fire started by sparks from a threshing engine ran east before a high wind for nearly twenty miles south of Moose Jaw, burning stacks, stables and one dwelling. Men turned out with wet sacks and ploughed guards, and the flames were finally stopped at the coulee. Loss is estimated at $8,000.
label: wildfire

text: PRINCE ALBERT, July 19, 1913. — Canoemen arriving from the north report that a great timber fire is raging along the Sturgeon River and has crossed to the north bank. Several trappers' cabins are believed lost. The fire is said to be burning on a front of fifteen miles, and its smoke has been plainly visible from the town for three days. The fur traders fear for their posts farther down the river.
label: wildfire

text: HEARST, Ont., June 18, 1923. The settlement narrowly escaped destruction on Saturday when a bush fire, fanned by a gale, came within half a mile of the station. Every able-bodied man was called out and a fire guard was cut through the spruce. Toward evening the wind veered and the danger passed, though smoke lay over the town for days afterward.
label: wildfire

text: Report of the Chief Fire Ranger for the season of 1914: ninety-three fires were recorded within the patrolled area, the greater number caused by settlers clearing land and by careless campers. The largest, in the Lac Seul country, burned over some 40 square miles of merchantable pine before it was checked by rains in mid-August. Fire lines were cut by crews of twelve to twenty men, and the canoe patrols were doubled on the main routes.
label: wildfire

text: Timber fire on the Gatineau limits, September 1909: three lumber camps burned, horses saved, no lives lost.
label: wildfire

text: My father always said the summer of 1929 was the year the bush came to the door. We were homesteading east of Bonnyville and it hadn't rained since May. One afternoon in August the sky to the west went brown, then orange, and ashes started falling like snow. We filled the cream cans with water, wet down the blankets and drove the cattle into the slough. The fire jumped the road and took the neighbour's barn and two miles of fence, but it went around our place. Six families lost everything that week, and the church basement in town was full of people for a month.
label: wildfire

text: FORT FRANCES, July 1926. The steamer arriving last evening brings news that bush fires are burning on both shores of Rainy Lake. Navigation was hampered by the dense smoke and the boat was obliged to tie up for twelve hours. Telegraph wires to the east are down. Passengers report that at one of the narrows the fire had reached the water's edge, and a settler's family was taken aboard from a rowboat after losing their house, stable and winter's supply of hay. Lumbermen fear heavy losses of standing pine on the limits along the north shore unless rain comes soon, and the town council has wired the government asking that more rangers be sent.
label: wildfire

text: A spark from a passing locomotive is blamed for the grass fire that burned over a large section of open range west of Fort Macleod, Alta., on April 22, 1911. Two ranchers lost their winter hay and about forty head of cattle perished. Mounted police organized parties to set back-fires along the trail. The fire travelled so fast before the west wind that riders sent to warn the ranches along the creek were barely ahead of it, and at one place it leaped the Oldman River where the water runs shallow over the gravel. A country schoolhouse was saved by the teacher and the older pupils, who beat out the burning grass with wet gunny sacks. The stockmen's association has asked the railway company to fit better spark arresters on its engines.
label: wildfire

text: ELK LAKE, Ont., May 30, 1931. Fire which broke out in slash north of the village yesterday has been brought under control after a hard fight. A crew of 150 men, rushed in by truck from the surrounding camps, held it at the river. One bridge was burned.
label: wildfire

text: Smoke from forest fires in the Nipigon country reported as far east as Port Arthur, August 1918. Fire still uncontrolled; rangers asking for more men.
label: wildfire

text: Season summary, Forest Service, 1934. Through the long summer more than four hundred fires were fought in the interior of British Columbia, the worst of them in the Quesnel and Chilcotin regions, where the timber had been left dry by a winter of light snow. Pumps, hose and pack horses were moved from one fire to the next. A series of lightning storms in late July set dozens of new fires in a single week, and smoke closed the Cariboo Road to motor traffic on three occasions.
label: wildfire

text: Three men employed by a lumber company perished when a forest fire overtook them in the woods north of Fort-Coulonge, Que., on June 7, 1903. Their bodies were found in a creek bed where they had sought refuge. The fire is still burning on a front of several miles. They had been sent up the river a week earlier to cruise timber on a new limit. Companions who escaped say the fire came down on the camp late in the afternoon with a roar like a train, driven by a strong west wind, and that the smoke was so thick a man could not see the next tree. Search parties were held back for a full day by the heat of the burning ground.
label: wildfire

text: A prairie fire, the worst in years, swept across the Qu'Appelle valley district on October 2, 1902, destroying grain in the stook, hay, granaries and a country schoolhouse. Settlers fought it all night with plough furrows and back-fires. Two families lost everything they owned and are being cared for by neighbours.
label: wildfire

text: NOTICE. Owing to the extreme fire hazard in the woods, all travel permits for the Temagami Forest Reserve are suspended until further notice. A fire of considerable size has been burning on the west arm of the lake since June 11, 1925, and every available ranger has been withdrawn to fight it.
label: wildfire

text: Bush fires still raging around Kirkland Lake; mine camps threatened; women and children sent out by special train. May 1924.
label: wildfire

text: Woods fires in Cumberland County, N.S., have burned over thousands of acres of blueberry barrens and young timber since the first week of May, 1930. Volunteers from the mining towns have been on the lines for ten days, and a mill and four farmhouses have been lost. It is believed the fires were set by the spring burning of blueberry ground, an old practice the government has often been asked to regulate. On Sunday the wind carried sparks over the railway into a lumber yard at the pithead, and the colliery whistle called the men up from below to fight it. Rain is promised for the end of the week.
label: wildfire

text: KAMLOOPS, B.C., August 1919. Range fires sweeping the parched hills north of the town have destroyed miles of fencing and the bunch-grass pasture on which several ranches depend for winter feed. Ranch hands and railway section crews have been set to fighting them, but the wind carries embers across every guard they cut.
label: wildfire

text: Forest fire hazard was extreme throughout northwestern Ontario during July 1955. On the 14th a lightning-caused fire near Sioux Lookout escaped initial attack and burned approximately 22,000 acres of jack pine and spruce before crews, aided by two Beaver aircraft fitted with water tanks, held it along a chain of lakes. No settlements were lost, but the railway main line was closed for a day by smoke.
label: wildfire

text: Grass fire, Assiniboia district, Sask., April 1957: three farmsteads burned, one elderly man dead, about 6,000 acres of stubble and pasture blackened.
label: wildfire

text: Radio message from the Fort Smith district office, June 1958: two fires burning out of control south of the Slave River, combined area estimated at 180 square miles. Smoke jumpers dropped at both. Requesting additional pumps and hose by first available aircraft. Weather hot and dry, winds southwest 20 to 25 m.p.h. No settlements threatened at this time.
label: wildfire

text: A crown fire roared through the lodgepole pine west of Edson on the afternoon of May 23, 1964, jumping the highway and racing toward the town before the wind swung around. Residents watched flames leaping a hundred feet above the treetops. Some 400 people were moved east by bus and train as a precaution, and the forestry branch called in bulldozers from the oil camps to widen the guard. Most of the timber destroyed was on crown land. Forestry officers said the spring had been so dry that the fire hazard had stood at extreme for nine days running before the fire was reported.
label: wildfire

text: Campers' carelessness is blamed for a forest fire which blackened about 3,000 acres in the eastern part of Algonquin Park during the second week of August, 1952. Canoe parties were warned off the lakes and three portages were closed. Lands and Forests crews, assisted by a provincial aircraft, report the fire is now under control.
label: wildfire

text: The towerman on Bald Mountain, near Mattawa, spotted the smoke at 2:40 in the afternoon of July 9, 1949, and by the time the first crew reached it on foot the fire had grown to some forty acres in heavy slash. It ran for three days before a change in the weather brought rain. The loss in standing timber on the company's limits is placed at nine million board feet. Two hundred men from the company's camps, armed with axes, shovels and portable pumps, held the fire along the line of a tote road. A cook and a teamster were treated for burns at the Mattawa hospital.
label: wildfire

text: Bush fire east of Flin Flon, July 1950. Power line to the mine cut for six hours. Approx. 15 sq. mi. burned.
label: wildfire

text: Water bombers of the provincial air service made more than a hundred drops on a fire threatening the village of Foleyet over the weekend of June 3, 1972, while bulldozers pushed a firebreak along the south edge of the townsite. Families were taken by train to Timmins as a precaution. The fire was reported held on Monday morning after burning about 9,000 acres. The fire started on the Thursday afternoon near the railway right-of-way, apparently from a spark, and was driven toward the village by a hot southwest wind gusting to 30 miles an hour. Officials said it was the third serious fire in the district in a month.
label: wildfire

text: SMOKE PALL OVER CITY. Smoke from scores of forest fires in eastern Manitoba and northwestern Ontario cast a yellow gloom over Winnipeg on August 22, 1946. Street lights came on in mid-afternoon and the weather office logged visibility of under a mile. The provincial forest service said more than 60 fires were burning, a dozen of them out of control.
label: wildfire

text: Spring 1940 brought a run of grass fires to southeastern Alberta. The worst began at a burning dump near Bow Island and, fanned by a chinook wind, spread over roughly 40 square miles of range before it was halted at an irrigation canal. Two homes and a community hall were destroyed. Officials blamed the bare, dry ground left by a winter with almost no snow for the speed of the fire. Farm families in the path of the fire took refuge in the irrigation ditches, and one rancher lost his whole stack yard and a dozen horses. The police estimated the damage at $40,000.
label: wildfire

text: Fire in the woods north of Baie-Comeau, July 1953: pulp company crews and village volunteers hold the blaze at the river after 4,000 acres burned.
label: wildfire

text: A forest fire which broke out near Bishop's Falls, Nfld., on June 11, 1971 burned through some 30 square miles of timber on the paper company's limits and forced 200 people from their homes for two nights. The forest service had 300 men on the fire line, along with tank trucks borrowed from neighbouring towns.
label: wildfire

text: I was posted at Molson Lake that summer, 1958. On the 2nd of August a thunderstorm went through without much rain, and next morning I counted eleven smokes from the tower. We had one Otter and two canoes. By the 5th they had joined into one fire running northeast, so we gave up on the head of it and concentrated on keeping it off the trading post and the settlement. We burned off a strip along the shore, soaked the roofs and moved the women and children onto the barges. On the 7th the wind turned and it burned back on itself. The post was saved. I don't think anybody ever measured how big it got.
label: wildfire

text: Two prospectors were rescued by float plane on September 1, 1966, after spending two days standing in a lake while a forest fire swept around them near Atikokan. Lands and Forests officials say the fire covered about 25,000 acres and is now being held. The men had lost their canoe, their packs and a summer's worth of samples. They told the pilot the heat on the water was so great they had to keep ducking under to wet their heads.
label: wildfire

text: Woods fire, Annapolis County, N.S., May 1946: two sawmills and nine dwellings destroyed; 150 volunteers on the lines.
label: wildfire

text: YELLOWKNIFE, N.W.T., July 1956. A forest fire that had been burning unchecked east of the Yellowknife River for nine days was turned back from the edge of the mine townsite on Sunday night. Miners off shift joined the forestry crew and cut a guard through the muskeg with axes and shovels. Ash fell on the town all weekend and the airstrip was closed by smoke. The fire had first been reported by a bush pilot on the 9th, and forestry officials blame an abandoned campfire on a portage. About 70 women and children were flown to Hay River as a precaution and will return when the smoke clears.
label: wildfire

text: A forest fire burned to within two miles of the Mayo townsite on June 27, 1951. Crews of miners and soldiers, ferried in by boat, cut a fireguard behind the village while residents loaded belongings onto a river barge. The fire, believed started by a careless camper on the Stewart River, eventually covered more than 60 square miles of spruce before rain fell on the 30th. Damage was confined to a sawmill, a woodcutter's camp and several miles of telephone line, but residents said they had never seen the sky so dark at midday in June.
label: wildfire

text: Bush fire forces evacuation. Wabowden, Man., May 1974: all 600 residents moved out by special train and road convoy as fire crosses the highway. Three houses and the school lost.
label: wildfire

text: GASPÉ, Que., August 1959. — For eleven days now the fire has been eating its way through the spruce and fir behind the coastal villages, and men who have fought it since the beginning say they have never seen woods so dry. It started, by most accounts, from a slash fire that was not properly put out. At its worst, on the 18th, it crossed two rivers in an afternoon and came down the hills toward the fishing settlements; the church bell rang at dusk and families carried their bedding down to the boats. Some 1,200 men are on the lines now, with bulldozers, portable pumps and two aircraft dropping water. Fourteen houses, a fish plant and two sawmills are gone. The provincial lands department estimates the burned area at 180 square miles.
label: wildfire

text: The Cypress Hills fire of late September 1938 began, according to the ranchers who first saw it, when a lightning strike set the dry grass alight on a bench above the creek. By the next day it had climbed into the pines. Before the snow came it had burned through a large part of the forest reserve and several thousand acres of grazing lease, and killed an unknown number of deer and elk.
label: wildfire
